newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Price reform seen bolstering South Korean refiners.
newsitem.headline: Price reform seen bolstering South Korean refiners.

text.p: South Korean oil refiners are likely to end up on a more solid financial footing after they quickly took advantage of a government green light on raising fuel oil prices, industry analysts said.
On January 1 the government freed price controls on domestic gasoline, kerosene, diesel and C-type fuel. These fuels will no longer be subject to a government-set monthly price ceiling.
Refiners wasted little time raising prices and analysts said the move will bolster profit margins and balance sheets and signals a focus on the domestic rather than export markets for the time being.
"Price hikes will help improve oil refiners' earnings structure in the refining sector," said Yong Han, an energy analyst at Jardine Fleming Securities.

Analysts said the perceived focus on domestic markets should be short-lived, however. In 1999 the government plans to open the refining sector to foreign companies -- the next major step in liberalising a sector that has been dominated by Korean conglomerates for decades.

The refiners, who process 2.4 million barrels per day of crude, said they raised petrol prices to counter high international prices for crude and foreign exchange losses caused by the won's eight percent fall against the dollar in 1996.
Petrol at the pump has risen two percent to 828-829 won (98 cents) per litre, from 815 won.

South Korean drivers had already been paying the most expensive prices in the nation's history after they were raised in December to 815 won per litre from 727 won -- the biggest rise since 1992 and the first time prices exceeded 800 won.
Kerosene prices have increased to 387-388 won a litre since January 1 from 346 won and diesel prices have risen to 382-385 won from 347 won.

Several analysts estimated the nation's five oil refiners lost a combined 350 billion won last year, compared with an 8.45 billion shortfall in 1995. Foreign exchange losses were cited as accounting for 70 percent of the total losses.
The petrol price rise has not drawn a response from the South Korean administration, which has retained a right to intervene if price volatility endangers the economy.
"We weren't surprised by the price hikes because we expected the oil companies to raise the prices to some degree," said an official at the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy.
"Crude oil prices and the won's depreciation have dealt a big blow to the oil firms financially, so they want compensation."
But the ministry expects prices to fall back when international crude prices ease, he said.
However, analysts said the refiners would be able to get away with not lowering their prices as much as crude prices.
"This is what companies will try to do to increase margins," said Bill Hunsaker, an energy analyst at ING-Barings Securities. "They will keep the margins despite the crude price fall."
With the added profits, analysts said the sector was likely to increase investments.
"The new investment would mostly go to upgrading facilities and petrochemical plants," said Han of Jardine Fleming.
In line with global trends, analysts said they expected refiners to invest in production of more environmentally friendly products. South Korea is placing increasingly stringent laws on oil products.
South Korea already produces net exports of petrochemicals, and is betting on Chinese demand to support expanding naphtha and petrochemical BTX production.
(Conversion $1 = 842 won)
